chunk: Irradiation with a mixed heavy ion beam induces ovarian follicle loss and dose-dependent mixed ovarian tumor development

paper_metadata.title: Irradiation with a mixed heavy ion beam induces ovarian follicle loss and dose-dependent mixed ovarian tumor development.

chunk: Over 25% of active NASA astronauts are women who will be exposed to low daily doses and dose rates of galactic cosmic rays (GCR) in space. We hypothesized that exposing mice to a preliminary simulated GCR mixed heavy ion beam composed of iron, silicon, and titanium ions induces follicle depletion and dose-dependent ovarian tumors. Female mice were exposed to 10, or 20 cGy each of Fe, Si, and Ti ions or sham-irradiation in quick succession within 15 min for total doses of 0, 30, or 60 cGy of the three beams. 16 months later, their ovaries were removed. Hyperplasia of the ovarian surface epithelium (OSE) was noted in 13%, 59%, and 22% of the 0, 30, and 60 cGy irradiated mice, respectively. The prevalence of mixed ovarian tumors was 0, 6, and 89%, respectively, in the 0, 30, and 60 cGy groups. Low numbers of Ki67 positive OSE and tumor cells supported a benign tumor phenotype. In a separate study, Si ion irradiation alone at 32 cGy did not induce ovarian tumors in mice; however, the mixed heavy ions at all doses and Si ion irradiation alone reduced the total number of healthy ovarian follicles. Mixed heavy ion exposure reduced lipid peroxidation, fibrosis, inflammation, and lipofuscin accumulation at 60 cGy compared to 0 cGy, but elevated inflammation and lipofuscin accumulation at 30 cGy compared to 60 cGy. Preliminary simulated GCR exposure causes ovarian follicle death and tumorigenesis. This study provides insight into space-radiation induced ovarian damage and cancer risk in females.
Graphical Abstract

Exposure to preliminary simulated GCR in the form of Si, Ti, and Fe ion irradiation induced follicle death and dose-dependent mixed ovarian tumor formation in mice, with the mixed heavy ion beam having a higher tumor prevalence compared to Si ions alone.

Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) are a type of radiation composed of mixed charged ions that may pose a serious threat to astronauts on prolonged space missions outside of Earth’s protective magnetic field. Galactic cosmic rays originating from supernova explosions outside of the solar system are composed of 85% protons, 14% alpha ions, and 1% high-charge (Z) and energy (E) ions (or HZE ions) [1]. HZE ions are responsible for 21% of the tissue dose equivalent from GCRs, which is the product of the absorbed dose (Gray, Gy, joules/kg) and the radiation weighting factor (2 for protons and 20 for alpha ions and heavy ions) [2–4]. HZE ions are significantly damaging due to their high linear energy transfer (LET), the amount of energy deposited into tissue per unit length of radiation travel. High-LET, HZE ions produce concentrated ionization events along a linear path, in contrast to low-LET ionization from x-rays or gamma radiation [5, 6]. Concentrated ionization events induce densely packed DNA double stranded breaks (DSBs) or clusters of DNA damage which are more detrimental to cells, partly by limiting DSB end protection and complicating DNA repair [7, 8]. Ion fluence, the number of particles received by a surface per unit area, like LET also has an effect on measuring biological damage caused by different ions at the same dose [1].

Our prior studies revealed that exposure of female mice to charged iron (Fe) or oxygen (O) ions, two prominent HZE ions, induced DSBs, oxidative lipid damage, and apoptosis in the ovary [9, 10]. These effects culminated in the destruction of ovarian follicles and the development of epithelial ovarian tumors in mice exposed to 50 cGy of Fe ions [9–11]. Dietary supplementation with alpha lipoic acid, an antioxidant, did not appreciably offset the negative effects observed in mice irradiated with 50 cGy of either O or Fe ions [9, 10]. Ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in women and estimated to cause over 19 000 deaths in 2023 [12]. The most frequent type of ovarian cancer, high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma accounts for 75% of ovarian carcinoma, and evidence has accumulated that the vast majority arise from the fallopian tubes [13]. Ovarian cancer is more common in post-menopausal women, due to the natural depletion of ovarian follicles and disruptions in the hypothalamic–pituitary-ovarian axis, which can lead to oxidative stress, inflammation and fibrosis in the ovaries [14]. While previous studies were focused on the effects of single heavy ion irradiation on the mammalian ovary, it is important to consider that astronauts in space are simultaneously exposed to multiple types of HZE ions at a time [1]. At solar minimum of the 11-year solar cycle, when GCR intensity is maximal, the GCR ion spectra includes HZE ions with atomic numbers ranging from 1 to 26 and varying fluence, among which silicon (Si, Z = 14), titanium (Ti, Z = 22), and Fe (Z = 26) are abundant [15, 16]. Of these ions, Fe ions are the largest contributors to GCR dose equivalent [16]. NASA is pushing the bounds of space exploration with a potential Mars mission (1000 days, 2.7 years) which is predicted to have an effective dose of 1070 mSV, a 5.1%-Risk of Exposure Induced Death, and an absorbed dose at 42 cGy for a 40-year-old female astronaut [17]. These numbers exceed the predicted doses experienced by female astronauts on a lunar mission (180 days) at 170 millisievert (mSv) and atomic bomb survivors at 1000 mSv, and the annual dose limits for the general public at 5 mSv and 50 mSv for nuclear powerplant workers [17–19]. Over a quarter of NASA astronauts eligible for flight assignment are women; therefore, advancing our knowledge on radiation-induced ovarian failure is critical for understanding health risks to astronauts and developing protective countermeasures. In this study we investigated how exposure to a mixed beam of Si, Ti, and Fe ions affected ovarian parameters, including ovarian follicle numbers, lipid peroxidation, inflammation, fibrosis, and tumor development. We hypothesized that this mixture of ions would significantly decrease the number of healthy ovarian follicles and induce ovarian tumors.

All animals in this study were cared for and housed in accordance with the National Research Council Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (1996) and the animal welfare standards incorporated in 9 CFR Part 3, 1991. Three-month-old female CB6F1/Hsd mice, a hybrid cross between BALB/cAnNHsd female and C57BL/6NHsd male mice (ENVIGO, Indianapolis, IN), were exposed to 0 (sham), 10 cGy or 20 cGy of Si, Ti, and Fe ions at energies of 260 MeV/u (dose-averaged LET = 70 KeV/μm), 1000 MeV/u (dose-averaged LET = 100 KeV/μm), and 600 MeV/u (dose-averaged LET = 193 KeV/μm), respectively, at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory, Brookhaven National Laboratory (NSRL, BNL; Upton, NY). These doses were chosen to bracket the estimated absorbed dose from GCRs that a 40-year-old female astronaut would experience in a spacecraft on a Mars mission [17]. The heavy ion beams were delivered to 419 experimental mice in quick succession in the order of lowest LET to highest LET (Si, Ti, Fe) for a total dose of 0, 30, or 60 cGy (n = 52, 0 cGy; n = 176, 30 cGy; n = 191, 60 cGy). In a separate experiment, mice of the same sex, strain and age were irradiated with 32 cGy of Si ions alone at an energy of 260 MeV/u (dose-averaged LET = 70 KeV/μm) or were sham irradiated (0 cGy). We note that there are several limitations to this study: ground-based ion beam radiation facilities can deliver only an approximate range of the mixed beams at low doses and dose-rates found in space travel and this study was not completed under fully simulated GCR nor microgravity conditions. After irradiation, the animals were shipped to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), where they were weighed monthly and were clinically observed for tumors. Animals with tumors were monitored and sacrificed as recommended by the attending LBNL veterinarian; tissue from moribund mice euthanized before study termination was collected at LBNL, shipped to SRI international for histological processing, and stored at the NASA Biological Institutional Scientific Collection (NBISC) at Ames Research Center. Tissues from moribund mice were not investigated in this study. The surviving animals were housed for 16 months at the Animal Barrier Facility at LBNL prior to transportation to SRI International for necropsy and tissue collection. Grossly normal appearing ovaries were formalin-fixed and stored in prelabeled screw top cryovial tubes. Subsequently, randomly selected bilateral, grossly normal-appearing ovaries from 16–18 mice per experimental group in the mixed beam experiment (representing a small percentage of the total number of samples from each group based on previous published work demonstrating statistically robust tumor prevalence) and 30 unilateral randomly selected ovaries per group from the Si experiment were shipped to the University of California, Irvine (UCI) for further studies [11]. Upon arrival, ovaries were washed in 50% ethanol three times and stored in 70% ethanol until further processing. Additionally, ovaries with grossly observable ovarian tumors were processed for pathology at LBNL and reviewed by a pathologist; subsequently they were shipped to NBISC at Ames Research Center and stored there before being shipped to UCI for histopathology. According to the NBISC records, a total of three mice exposed to 30 cGy (3 of n = 176) and nine mice exposed to 60 cGy (9 of n = 191) of the mixed heavy ion beam developed gross ovarian tumors; however, upon histological and molecular characterization of purported gross ovarian tumors only 1 mouse in the 30 cGy and five mice in the 60 cGy group were confirmed to have ovarian tumors. The remaining samples, two purported ovarian samples from the 30 cGy group and four purported ovarian samples from the 60 cGy group were determined to not be ovarian tissues and were thus excluded from further analyses.

Formalin-fixed, normal appearing ovaries from the mixed ions and Si ion studies were embedded in 20 and 15 paraffin blocks, respectively. Each block contained five ovaries and one piece of uterus for position reference. These blocks were serially sectioned at 5 μm thickness. Every sixth slide was stained with Shandon Gill 3 hematoxylin and eosin Y (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA) for blocks 1–15 of the mixed ions study. Every fifth slide of blocks 15–20 from the mixed ions study and all blocks from the Si ion study were stained with Gill’s hematoxylin and eosin-Y. The stained slides were examined for abnormalities using light microscopy, blind to the treatment group by one of the authors (GL), a board-certified veterinary pathologist. The remaining sections were used for immunohistochemical analysis.

Using the ovaries from mice without gross tumors, follicles were classified and counted in every fifth section of hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides from the first 23 ovaries of the mixed ions study by an investigator (KG-A) blind to the treatment group. Follicles were counted at every fifth section for the first 12 ovaries of the Si ion study by an investigator (LB) blind to treatment groups. This is about six to seven animals per treatment group, which was an “n” based on published studies [9, 10]. Healthy primordial (single layer of flattened pre-granulosa cells with at most one cuboidal cell), primary (single layer of mixed flattened and cuboidal cells or all cuboidal granulosa cells), secondary (more than one and less than five layers of cuboidal granulosa cells), and antral (more than four layers of cuboidal granulosa cells and containing an antral cavity) follicles were counted using an Olympus BX60 Light Microscope (Tokyo, Japan) [20, 21]. The remaining ovarian sections from the mice exposed to 0, 30, and 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam were used to perform immunohistochemistry. One of the markers analyzed was phosphorylated H2A.X variant histone (γH2AX), a marker for DNA damage. Because these animals had very few ovarian follicles, 1–2 sections per animal were selected for this endpoint, specifically choosing section numbers that bracketed the known location of a previously counted follicle to maximize detection. In total, 20 ovarian sections from 3–6 mice per treatment group were investigated to quantify γH2AX-negative and γH2AX-positive primordial, primary, secondary, and antral follicles. These numbers were used to find the percentage of γH2AX positive follicles per treatment group as previously recorded in our published work [9, 10].

Formalin-fixed, paraffin embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized in Histoclear and rehydrated with ethanol, water, and PBS before they were incubated in 10 mmol/L sodium citrate with 0.05% Tween 20 at 95°C, blocked with avidin/biotin blocking reagents and PBS-diluted animal serum (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA). If the primary antibody was from a rabbit, mouse, or goat—PBS-diluted goat, mouse, or rabbit serum was used for blocking, respectively. After this, tissues were incubated with primary antibodies raised against epithelial marker Pancytokeratin (Type II cytokeratins 1, 5, 6, and 8) [20, 22], mitosis-specific protein Ki67 [23], lipid peroxidation marker 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) [24], granulosa cell marker forkhead box protein L2 (FOXL2) [25], or theca cell marker cytochrome P450 family 17 subfamily a polypeptide 1 (CYP17A1) [26], followed by respective secondary antibodies (Table 1). After secondary antibody incubation, the sections were further blocked with 0.3% H2O2 and treated with ABC reagent (Vector Laboratories). Visualization was performed with diaminobenzidine (DAB) substrate in peroxide buffer (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN), and slides were counterstained with hematoxylin. The stained tissues were then dehydrated in ethyl alcohol (Gold Shield, Hayward, CA) and Histo-clear before mounting with Permount mounting medium (Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, PA). Immunohistochemistry was conducted blind to treatment groups and using 1–3 ovarian sections per animal; data from these slides were averaged per animal. Images of ovarian sections were taken with a BX60 Olympus Light Microscope, Retiga 2000R Camera System, and Q-Capture Pro Software. The images were then transferred to FIJI (NIH) and subjected to auto white balancing and image analysis. Briefly, the freeform selection tool was used to manually obtain ovarian section area from which follicles and corpora lutea were omitted, ovarian tubular adenoma area, and lipofuscin positive areas. The length of the OSE was measured using the freehand line tool in FIJI. To measure 4-HNE staining intensity, images of treated ovarian sections were used to manually select the ovarian section area (follicles and corpora lutea omitted) and color deconvoluted to split DAB and hematoxylin dyes into separate color channels [27]. Using the DAB color channel and the mean grey value provided by FIJI the intensity of 4-HNE-positive ovarian section area was determined (follicles and corpora lutea omitted) [27]. These analyses were conducted in line with our previously published work and for ovaries without gross ovarian tumors [27].

Picrosirius-red staining (PSR) was done following a protocol from Briley et al., 2016 and Brehm and Flaws 2021 originating from the Dr. Francesca Duncan laboratory at Northwestern University [28, 29]. Briefly, tissues were deparaffinized in Histoclear and rehydrated with ethanol and water before submerging the tissues in a solution composed of 0.1% Sirius Red F3b, direct red 80 and 1.3% picric acid (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO). After this, the tissues were placed in a solution of 0.05 N HCL in water. Next, the tissues were dehydrated with ethanol and Histoclear before mounting onto slides. PSR staining and analysis were completed blind to experimental treatment group and using 1–2 ovarian sections per animal; data from these slides were averaged per animal. Images of each ovarian section were imported into FIJI, the ovarian tissue area (minus follicles and corpora lutea area) was manually selected with the freeform line tool, and PSR positive areas were recorded using the thresholding function as described by the online user guide [30].

Tissue slides were deparaffinized in Histoclear and rehydrated with ethanol, water, and PBS before they were incubated in 10 mmol/l sodium citrate with 0.05% Tween 20 at 95°C (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO). The tissues were then incubated with anti-CD68 antigen (CD68) overnight at 4°C (Table 1). The following day the tissue slides were washed with PBS and incubated with goat-anti rabbit Alexa 633 fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies. Autofluorescence was reduced with the ReadyProbes tissue autofluorescence quenching kit (ThermoFisher, Waltham, MA). The nuclei of cells were visualized with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI). CD68 immunofluorescence and analysis was completed blind to experimental treatment group and using 1–2 ovarian sections per animal. Tissues were imaged with a 405 nm (to visualize DAPI) and 633 nm (to visualize Alexa 633) laser with an emission spectrum of 436–473 and 642–671 nm, respectively on the SP8 Leica confocal microscope (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany) at UCI’s Optical Biology Core (Irvine, CA). After the ovarian section area (follicles and corpora lutea omitted) was manually outlined with the freeform tool, the CD68 positive area was calculated using FIJI’s thresholding function after importing processed images from IMARIS software (Oxford Instruments). Using the same microscope system, lipofuscin autofluorescence was imaged using a 488 nm laser and an emission spectrum of 505–700 nm. The brightfield overlay images were taken using a photomultiplier tube. The ovarian section area and lipofuscin positive areas were manually selected using FIJI’s freeform tool to calculate the ratio of lipofuscin to ovarian section area.

Prevalence of each observed ovarian pathology per treatment group was calculated by dividing the number of mice with a given pathology over the total number of mice in that treatment group. Continuous data such as follicle counts, cell counts, area, and staining intensities were subjected to a nonparametric Kruskal–Wallis test to analyze differences among groups, followed by Mann Whitney or Dunn’s test for intergroup comparisons if the Kruskal Wallis test p-value was less than 0.05. Data expressed as counts by treatment group were analyzed using Fisher’s Exact test. The Si study had two groups; because of this, continuous data were statistically analyzed using a Student’s t-test. The program SPSS 20 for Windows or SPSS 23 for Macintosh (IBM Corporation) was used for all statistical analyses.

A schematic of ovarian follicle development is shown in Figure 1A. At 19 months of age and 16 months after irradiation, there is a trend to lower number of healthy follicles (sum of morphologically healthy primordial, primary, secondary, and antral in ovaries with representative images in Figure 1C) in mice exposed to 30 cGy (5.0 ± 1.8) and 60 cGy (6.9 ± 3.6) of the mixed heavy ion beam, compared to control mice (17.6 ± 3.1) (Kruskal-Wallis, P = 0.0362; 0 v 30 cGy P = 0.0514; 0 v 60 cGyp = 0.0623, 30 v 60 cGy P = 0.873, Dunn’s test, Figure 1D). The average number of antral follicles was significantly decreased in the 30 and 60 cGy groups compared to control mice (Kruskal-Wallis, P = 0.0413; 0 v 30 cGy P = 0.0427, Dunn’s test; 0 v 60 cGy P = 0.0338, Dunn’s test). The percent of total ovarian follicles that were positive for γH2AX were not altered by radiation treatment (Supplementary Figure 1). The numbers of primordial, primary, and secondary follicles were not statistically altered (Kruskal-Wallis, P > 0.05). Si irradiated mice (representative images in Figure 1B) experienced a significant depletion of the sum of healthy follicles of all stages compared to sham-irradiated mice (0 cGy: 70.7 ± 12.8, 32 cGy: 8.67 ± 1.85, Mann Whitney, P = 0.004, N = 6 mice/treatment; Figure 1E). Average numbers of primordial, primary, and secondary were significantly decreased in mice exposed to Si ions alone compared to control mice (Mann Whitney, P ≤ 0.05). Antral follicle numbers were not significantly altered by Si exposure (Mann Whitney, P > 0.05). Overall, follicle numbers were low in both studies, as expected in mice of advanced age [31].

Capsular hyperplasia, salpingitis, and ovarian atrophy were noted in ovaries retrieved from mice irradiated with 0, 30, or 60 cGy of Si, Ti, and Fe ions. The OSE is normally composed of a single layer of epithelial cells, which ruptures during ovulation and is repaired thereafter. Capsular hyperplasia describes excessive proliferation of the OSE, and it was observed in 13%, 59%, and 22% of the 0, 30, and 60 cGy irradiated mice, respectively (P = 0.003, Fisher’s Exact Test, Table 2). Salpingitis is the inflammation of the oviduct, and it was noted in 13%, 12%, and 11% of the mice irradiated with 0, 30, and 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam (P = 0.943, Fisher’s Exact Test, Table 2). The complete absence of ovarian tissue was defined as ovarian atrophy and was not statistically altered with dose (P = 0.424, Fisher’s Exact Test, Table 2). Pathologies of this nature were not observed in mice exposed to 0 or 32 cGy of Si ions.

In this study, a subset of ovarian samples were randomly selected from a larger study under the LBNL program. Results from these samples showed that the prevalences of ovarian tumors after exposure to 0, 30, or 60 cGy of mixed ions were 0%, 6% or 95% respectively, suggesting that ovarian tumorigenesis is dose-dependent (P < 0.001, Fisher’s Exact Test, Table 2). Only one mouse out of 17 mice in the 30 cGy group had a unilateral tumor (6%) and 16 (94%) had no ovarian tumors. 11% of mice in the 60 cGy group did not have tumors, 33% of mice in the 60 cGy group had unilateral tumors, and 56% had bilateral tumors (Figure 2A). The prevalence of unilateral or bilateral tumors was scored after pathological analysis of H&E-stained sections. The tumors were then molecularly categorized with antibodies against Pancytokeratin, FOXL2, and CYP17A1. These proteins are markers of three critical somatic cell types of the ovary: epithelial, granulosa, and theca cells. Pancytokeratin monoclonal antibody targets cytokeratin 1, 5, 6, and 8, which are proteins found on epithelial cells [20, 22]. As expected, all mice had a Pancytokeratin positive OSE regardless of treatment group (Figure 3A). All tumors observed in irradiated mice were classified as Pancytokeratin positive ovarian tubular adenomas, which describes tumors that are believed to have formed from the abnormal invagination or downgrowth of the OSE (also referred to as germinal epithelium) [32, 33]. Ovarian tubular adenomas are specific to mice and not found in humans. Ovarian tubular adenomas are characterized by tubular structures, and the cells lining the tubules were Pancytokeratin positive in both 30 (Figure 3A) and 60 cGy (Figure 3B) treatment groups, confirming their epithelial origin. To further characterize the cell(s) of origin in these tumors, specifically the cells in pockets between Pancytokeratin-positive tubules which are Pancytokeratin-negative, antibodies against proteins FOXL2 and CYP17A1 were used. FOXL2 is a critical transcription factor expressed in the nuclei of granulosa cells of maturing follicles. CYP17A1, localized within theca cell cytoplasm in the ovary, is an enzyme of the steroidogenesis pathway that is responsible for converting pregnenolone into dehydroepiandrosterone. Only 11% of mice in the 60 cGy group had FOXL2 positive, CYP17A1 negative tumors (Figure 3C). The one unilateral tumor found in a mouse of the 30 cGy group had CYP17A1 positive, FOXL2 negative cells between the tubular structures of the tubular adenoma, while this was observed in 6% of mice of the 60 cGy group (Figure 3C). Looking at these two markers together, 72% of mice in the 60 cGy group had tumors that were positive for both FOXL2 and CYP17A1, specifically the cells in between the tubular structures of the tubular adenoma (Table 2). We noted the staining pattern of FOXL2 and CYP17A1 positive cells in the tumors of irradiated mice, specifically whether the positive cells were concentrated in a smaller area of the tumor or scattered throughout the tumor area (Table 3). Of the mice in the 60 cGy group, 39% and 44% had scattered and focused FOXL2 positive cells in the tumor area, respectively (Figure 3D). Most mice had scattered CYP17A1 positive cells in the tumor area with 6% and 50% in the 30 cGy and 60 cGy group mixed-beam groups, respectively (Figure 3D). Few mice had CYP17A1 positive cells in a focused pattern, with 22% of mice in the 60 cGy group. Of the mice in the 60 cGy group, 88% had more than 5 FOXL2 positive cells within the tumor area (Table 3), while only 40% had more than 5 CYP17A1 positive cells within the tumor area (Figure 3D). Mice irradiated with 32 cGy Si alone did not develop ovarian tumors. Grossly abnormal ovaries, 1 mouse in the 30 cGy and five mice in the 60 cGy group, were analyzed separately from ovaries of mice that had apparently normal ovaries at necropsy. Upon pathological and molecular characterization, an ovarian hemangioma was observed in the mouse from the 30 cGy group. Of the mice in the 60 cGy group, two had mixed ovarian tumors. Of those two mice one had an ovarian tubular adenoma and hemangioma, while the other had a granulosa cell tumor and an ovarian tubular adenoma. The third mouse had an ovarian tubular adenoma while the two remaining mice had granulosa cell tumors. The gross ovarian tumors diagnosed as ovarian tubular adenomas had similar morphological and molecular staining patterns to those from mice that did not develop grossly visible tumors (Supplementary Figure 2).

To determine whether the cells of the OSE or tubular adenoma were actively dividing in the ovaries of mice across treatment groups, we counted the number of Ki67 positive cells divided by the OSE length and ovarian tubular adenoma area, respectively (Figure 4A). There were no statistically significant differences in the number of Ki67 positive cells over the length of the OSE among the treatment groups (Kruskal-Wallis Test P = 0.704, Figure 4B). Consistent with few Ki67-positive cells, there were also very few cells with mitotic figures in the tubular adenomas. The number of Ki67-positive cells divided by the area of tubular adenomas was not significantly altered across the treatment groups (Kruskal-Wallis, P = 0.424, Figure 4C).

4-HNE is a byproduct of lipid peroxidation, a process that occurs when excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) oxidize polyunsaturated fatty acids in cellular membranes. ROS are generated from the ionization of water by ionizing radiation [24, 34, 35]. We previously reported increased 4-HNE immunopositivity in ovarian granulosa cells and oocytes of follicles at 6 h and one week after irradiation with O or Fe ions [9, 10]. To determine whether persistently increased lipid peroxidation could be observed 16-months after mixed heavy ion beam irradiation we probed the ovarian tissue with an antibody against 4-HNE (Figure 5A). Comparing 4-HNE staining intensities across treatment groups we found a decrease that is borderline statistically significant in the 60 cGy group compared to the sham-irradiated mice (P = 0.098, Kruskal Wallis; 0 v 60, P = 0.022, Mann Whitney, Figure 5B). PSR staining is a method to detect the presence of collagen I and III fibers in tissue, thereby allowing investigators to observe potential changes in collagen. Collagens I and III appear red while PSR negative areas are yellow (Figure 5C). Quantifying the ratio of PSR positive area to ovarian area from irradiated and control groups revealed 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam showed borderline statistically significant reduction in collagen I and III levels when compared to control mice (P = 0.051, Kruskal Wallis test; 0 v 60 cGy P = 0.017, Mann–Whitney U, Figure 5D).

Lipofuscin has been localized in ovaries of aging humans, mice, rabbits, fish, and monkeys [36–40]. Oxidative stress is associated with aging and is a contributor to ovarian lipofuscin accumulation [41]. We found that the lipofuscin positive area in relation to ovarian stroma area (excluding ovarian follicles and corpora lutea) was reduced with borderline statistical significance in the 60 cGy group when compared to control mice (P = 0.098, Kruskal Wallis; 0 vs 60, P = 0.004, Mann Whitney, Figure 6A and B). Additionally, we observed that this ratio was significantly higher in ovaries of mice exposed to the 30 cGy versus 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam (30 vs 60, P = 0.002, Mann Whitney, Figure 6B). An antibody against CD68, an M1 pro-inflammatory macrophage marker, was used on ovarian tissues from the three treatment groups to assess any persistent inflammatory responses 16 months after irradiation (Figure 6C). M1 macrophages are important during normal ovarian physiology and human ovarian cancer initiation, regardless of the cell of origin: the OSE or cells of the fallopian tubes [42–44]. After calculating the ratio of CD68 positive area to ovarian stroma area we found that this ratio is significantly higher in mice of the 0 and 30 cGy group compared to mice in the 60 cGy group (P = 0.013, Kruskal Wallis; 0 vs 60 cGy, P = 0.031; 30 vs 60, P = 0.010, Mann Whitney; Figure 6D). Lipofuscin is often called an “age pigment”, as it is an accumulation of cross-linked, oxidized, undigested proteins in lysosomes of CD68 positive macrophages and other cells [45, 46].

Our understanding of ground-based radiation health effects stems from epidemiological studies that follow radiation-exposed industrial workers, atomic bomb survivors and radiation therapy recipients. The Life Span Study, which follows a cohort of atomic bomb survivors after the events of World War II (1958–2009), evaluated the association between gamma radiation and ovarian cancer [47, 48]. Utada et al. 2020 established a positive association between gamma radiation exposure and risk of high-grade serous (Type II), but not low-grade serous (Type 1) ovarian cancers [48]. With the prospect of extended space exploration in the near future, there is increasing concern about the health effects of extended exposure to space radiation. In this study, we investigated the effects of a mixed heavy ion beam consisting of 10 or 20 cGy each of Si, Ti, and Fe ions, which partly models GCR exposure in space, on the mouse ovary. Additionally, we probed the effects of 32 cGy of a single dose of a single highly energetic heavy ion (Silicon ions) on the mouse ovary. We found that the three beam mixed heavy ion beam decreased ovarian follicle numbers and dose-dependently induced ovarian tumorigenesis. 32 cGy of Si ions alone decreased total healthy ovarian follicle numbers; however, no histopathologies or tumors were observed. In addition, 30 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam increased the percent of mice with ovarian capsular hyperplasia when compared to sham irradiated mice and mice irradiated with 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam, consistent with capsular hyperplasia being a precursor lesion to ovarian tumor development. Supplementing these observations, few mitotic figures were observed in the OSE and ovarian tubular adenomas of irradiated mice, supporting the benign nature of the tumors. To investigate the role of the mixed heavy ion beam on additional factors that may influence ovarian tumor development we measured oxidative stress and general inflammatory response by quantifying proteins 4-HNE and CD68. We also assessed lipofuscin and collagen content, which are histological signs of senescence. Overall, this study adds to the body of evidence regarding the dangers of space radiation on female ovarian health.

High-LET radiation destroys ovarian follicles by causing DNA damage, oxidative damage, and apoptosis [9]. Our laboratory previously found a significant increase in the percentage of primordial follicles containing γH2AX positive oocytes 6 h after exposure to 50 cGy of Fe ions [9]. This effect was resolved 1-week post-exposure. The significant DNA damage triggered apoptotic elimination of affected primordial follicles, as indicated by PUMA positive oocytes in 12-week-old C57BL6J mice 1 week after exposure. Overall, 50 cGy of Fe ions significantly depleted primordial follicles at 1 week, with an even greater reduction by 8 weeks post-exposure. Despite the mice in this study being 19 months old at the time of necropsy, an age at which CB6F1 mice already exhibit a lower number of ovarian follicles, we observed an appreciably lower total number of healthy follicles in irradiated mice (mixed ion and Si beam) compared to control mice. We wondered if DNA damage would persist in the remaining follicles of our mice since other researchers have found that 11–12 month old Friends leukemia virus B mice, mice that experience a significant decline in ovarian follicles starting at 4–5 weeks of age, harbor a higher percentage of primordial follicles positive for γH2AX compared to 4–5 week old control mice [49]. However, in our 19-month-old mice we found only a single secondary follicle was positive for γH2AX out of 18 total follicles in the 0 cGy group. Only seven follicles were identified in the 30 cGy group, none of which were positive for γH2AX, and the 60 cGy group had no follicles at all. The interpretation of this endpoint is limited by very low ovarian follicle numbers across the three treatment groups due to both age and radiation induced depletion. Future studies should calculate the ED50 for follicle destruction by the mixed and single beams at 6 h and 1-week post-irradiation in reproductively young and aged mice. This would help confirm the apoptotic elimination of oxidatively-stressed and DNA-damaged follicles by the mixed beam and determine the potency of mixed versus single heavy ion beams in follicle destruction. Nonetheless, premature loss of ovarian follicles is implicated in earlier onset of menopause and an increased risk of ovarian cancer infertility, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and neurological disease [14, 50, 51]. These findings emphasize the reproductive and long-term health risks of space radiation exposure to women.

We demonstrated that the mixed heavy ion beam induced a high prevalence of ovarian tubular adenomas at 60 cGy. We also observed a higher prevalence of mice with capsular hyperplasia in the 30 cGy group (59%) compared to the 0 cGy (13%) and 60 cGy (22%) groups. This difference is likely explained by the low prevalence of tumors in the 30 cGy (6%) group compared to the 60 cGy (89%) group. Capsular hyperplasia is believed to be the precursor lesion that precedes ovarian tubular adenoma development after radiation exposure. The high prevalence of capsular hyperplasia in mice exposed to 30 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam suggests that these mice would likely have developed tubular adenomas if aged for a longer period after irradiation. Another important observation was the minimal Ki67 positive cells observed in the OSE and tubular adenomas, consistent with the latter’s benign nature [11]. Although ovarian tubular adenomas are specific to mice and do not occur in humans, their benign phenotype closely resembles human type I epithelial ovarian tumors rather than human type II epithelial ovarian tumors. Ninety percent of ovarian tumors in women are classified epithelial ovarian cancers [12, 52]. It is important to note that epithelial ovarian cancers were previously believed to originate from the OSE. More recent research supports that high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas predominantly arise from epithelial cells of the Fallopian tube that travel to the ovary, not from the surface epithelium [53]. In this scenario, the precursor lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma or STICs which are strongly associated with human type II epithelial ovarian tumors [53].

To enable a more detailed identification of tumors than prosector analysis alone, we used comprehensive histological and molecular marker analysis which is a key strength of this study. Mishra et al. 2018 were the first to identify mixed OTAs/granulosa cell tumors in mice exposed to charged Fe ions via molecular characterization with immunohistochemistry. Our molecular characterization analysis showed that the mixed heavy ion beam induced mixed tumors of epithelial, granulosa, and theca cell origin in mice. In our sham-irradiated mice, FOXL2 was only expressed in the nuclei of granulosa cells in growing ovarian follicles. By contrast, 83% of mice exposed to 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam had FOXL2 positive cells located only within the OTA, specifically in between the FOXL2 negative tubules. In the ovary CYP17A1 is an enzyme produced by theca cells, which is responsible for converting pregnenolone into dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), both intermediates of estradiol production. CYP17A1 is expressed in the theca cells of large antral follicles in mice, and in this study, we did not observe CYP17A1 positive theca cells surrounding large antral follicles in control and irradiated mice. Using ovaries from younger mice at 4 weeks old as a positive control, we clearly identified CYP17A1 positive theca cells surrounding large antral follicles (Supplementary Figure 3). Six percent of mice irradiated with 30 cGy and 72% of mice irradiated with 60 cGy of the mixed beam had CYP17A1 positive cells located within the ovarian tubular adenoma area. The high prevalence of mixed tumors, rather than tumors arising from a single cell type, may be explained by premature follicle death induced by heavy-ion irradiation. Evidence supports that the types of tumors that develop in the mouse ovary differ if the tumors are induced versus spontaneous and are influenced by gonadotropin hormones. Mice that experience premature follicle depletion due to aging, exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or mutations develop ovarian tubular adenomas [11, 20, 54, 55]. Tubular adenomas, which are hormonally inactive, are common in experimental models that experience germ cell deficiency or follicle depletion, studies report this in 56 to 95% of mice [55–59]. On the other hand, studies find that hormonally active ovarian tumors such as granulosa cell tumors, theca cell tumors, theca-granulosa cell tumors, and luteomas, form a majority of spontaneous growths in mice [32]. Genetically modified mice with elevated gonadotropin levels also develop granulosa cell tumors or luteomas, not tubular adenomas [59–61]. By contrast, hypogonadal mice lacking gonadotropins exhibit follicle loss but do not develop adenoma nor granulosa cell tumors 10–15 months after gamma irradiation [62]. We were unable to measure the concentration of gonadotropin hormones from serum of mice in our study; however, previous work in our laboratory established a significant increase in FSH and LH concentrations in serum from mice 8 weeks after exposure to 50 cGy of O or Fe ions [9, 10]. Follicle death followed by gonadotropin dysregulation may explain one path to mixed ovarian tumorigenesis by heavy ion irradiation.

Our previous work found that 50 cGy of Fe ion radiation significantly depleted ovarian follicles just one week after exposure in 12 week old mice and induced unilateral and bilateral ovarian tubular adenomas in 47% and 7% of 15-month old C57BL/6 J mice, respectively [11]. 60 cGy of mixed Si, Ti, and Fe heavy ion beam in the present study induced unilateral and bilateral tubular adenomas in 33% and 56% of mice, respectively. This suggests that 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam is a more potent inducer of bilateral ovarian tumors than 50 cGy of Fe alone. The tissue in the present study was acquired from NASA’s tissue sharing program, and there are therefore unavoidable differences between these two studies, which complicate direct comparisons in the tumor prevalences. These limitations include differences in mouse strain (C57BL/6 J vs CB6F1 in the present study), time after irradiation (15 vs 16 months post-irradiation in the present study), age at euthanasia (18 vs 19 months in the present study, LET for Fe 179 keV/μm vs 193 keV/μm), and radiation dose (50 vs 60 cGy in the present study). We also analyzed the effects of 32 cGy of Si ion irradiation alone at three-months of age on ovarian tumor prevalence at 19 months in CB6F1 mice. We observed no ovarian tumors at 16 months post Si-irradiation alone. Variability in tumor prevalence depends on ion velocity, energy, and charge, which influence LET and flux, which all play a role in determining potency of ions relative to each other. Together these data highlight the importance of beam quality, potential increased danger, and dose-dependence of a mixed heavy ion beam compared to single ion beams. To better model GCR exposures in space, future studies should focus on administering a series of lower doses over time and utilizing a mixed beam that better simulates the composition of GCRs [63]. As of 2020, NASA has developed a GCR simulator capable of exposing animal and cellular models to 33 sequential beams of protons, alpha ions, and HZE ions in similar proportions as they occur in GCRs in space [15]. Microgravity or weightlessness is another factor that should be considered in future studies as astronauts encounter this hazard during space travel and many studies have found that it disrupts endocrine signaling and ovarian function [64, 65]. Information gathered in these studies will provide important data to further advance the development of accurate models to characterize the absorbed doses to space travelers and design adequate shielding to protect space travelers for the long duration trip from Earth to Mars [63].

To understand the factors that underlie ovarian tumor formation after heavy ion irradiation-induced ovarian follicle loss, we sought to analyze factors that increase during ovarian aging and which are thought to play a role in epithelial ovarian cancer initiation in women [66–68] and are observed in the aging mouse ovary [29, 41, 54, 69]. Those factors are oxidative stress, fibrosis, and inflammation. We hypothesized that these factors would be higher in irradiated mice when compared to control mice; however, we saw a significant decrease in mice irradiated with 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam when compared to control mice. These results prompt future studies that test additional intermediate doses (e.g., 40 and 50 cGy) and earlier post-irradiation time points to better define the mechanisms driving tumor prevalence.

Lipid peroxidation, a process that occurs during oxidative stress, is driven by excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) [70]. ROS attack lipid structures by stealing their electrons to form oxidation products such as lipid hydroperoxides, which further break down into toxic aldehyde products like 4-HNE [24]. When cells are struck by ionizing radiation all their molecules are in danger of the loss of electrons, and this includes water of the cytoplasm. Water radiolysis, ionization of water, creates unstable radicals such as H2O+ [71]. This molecule can react with neighboring water molecules to create hydroxyl radicals (HO∙). Antioxidants are responsible for neutralizing ROS. When a large enough imbalance between antioxidants and ROS occurs, oxidative damage occurs, and cells undergo apoptosis or necrosis to be cleared from tissues. 12-week-old mice irradiated with 50 cGy of Fe ions had a significantly higher percent of 4-HNE positive oocytes in primordial, primary, and secondary follicles 6 h and 1 week after exposure compared to control mice [9]. In the present study, we observed a decreased 4-HNE intensity in ovarian sections of mice in the 60 cGy group compared to the 0 cGy group, with no significant difference between the control and 30 cGy group or the 30 and 60 cGy group. This pattern may be explained by the very low numbers of ovarian follicles at 19 months. Markers of oxidative lipid, protein, and DNA damage increase in the theca cells and granulosa cells of ovarian follicles in unexposed mice from 2 to 12 months of age [41]. Another important variable to consider is the higher prevalence of tumors, which covered most if not all the ovarian area, in the 60 cGy group. According to the Warburg effect, ATP is mainly produced via aerobic glycolysis not oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells, which is also true for ovarian cancer [72]. This metabolic switch is progressive as normal cells become benign tumors and benign tumors become malignant as shown by using an in vitro mouse surface epithelial cancer model [73, 74]. High oxidative stress and hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment does not enable cancer cells to die on their own, instead antioxidant defense mechanisms are deployed in ovarian cancer and contribute to chemotherapy resistance [72, 75]. The role of oxidative stress in the development of heavy ion induced ovarian tumors should be further investigated.

We also sought to probe the possibility of fibrosis being a factor important to ovarian tubular adenoma in mice after radiation induced ovarian follicle loss. We found a significant depletion of collagen in ovaries of mice exposed to 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam compared to control mice, but there were no significant differences between other groups. Some studies reported that fibrosis, measured via PSR, increases with age, 6–12 weeks old compared to 14–17 months old CD1 and CB6F1 mice, and 11–20 year old women compared to 57 year old women [29, 68, 76]. Ovaries from B6C3F1 mice injected with vinylcyclohexene diepoxide, a chemical that promotes follicle degeneration and tubular hyperplasia (tubular adenoma), showed changes in collagen shape, quantity, and organization before compared to after being injected using second harmonic generation microscopy [77]. At six months the ovary showed normal, tightly packed, thin, and linear collagen fibers; however, at the 13 month time point collagen was sparse, tangled, and curved fibers were present alongside tubular hyperplasia [77]. Moreover, collagens I and III content measured via PSR were significantly lower in benign ovarian tumors compared to stage III tumors in humans, while stage IV tumors had significantly less collagen than stage II tumors [78]. Another study reported that 1 Gy of gamma radiation in 8 weeks old mice did not cause changes in PSR staining; however, these results were not quantified via image analysis [79]. In the present study, 4-HNE and PSR positivity were reduced in ovaries of mice exposed to 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam, while no differences were observed between the 0 and 30 cGy groups. These findings provide evidence to support that decreased collagen in ovarian tissue of the 60 cGy group is a result of advanced tumor growth which occupied most, if not all, of the ovarian tissue and these tumors were largely PSR negative. In the future it would be informative to investigate how heavy ion radiation affects collagen content and arrangement in each of the ovarian extracellular matrix compartments (e.g., stroma, follicles, OSE) over time and after follicle loss and tumor growth.

Inflammation plays a role in epithelial ovarian cancer initiation by stimulating the tumor microenvironment, promoting genetic instability, and increasing ROS production, macrophage infiltration, and cytokine release, which can contribute to the transformation of OSE or distal fallopian tube cells into ovarian cancer [42, 43]. M1, pro-inflammatory macrophages initially respond to newly formed tumor cells by releasing anti-angiogenic factors, immuno-stimulatory chemokines, and phagocytosing tumor cells [80]. Knowing inflammation plays a role in ovarian cancer initiation, we asked whether we would see M1 macrophage populations in irradiated ovaries with a well-known M1 macrophage marker, CD68. DNA damage, oxidative stress, and follicle death are acute effects; and we expected to observe more macrophages in irradiated mouse ovaries compared to control mice as a long-term effect; however, we noted the mean ratio of CD68 positive area to ovarian area was significantly higher in the 30 cGy group than the 60 cGy group, but no different from the control group. Additionally, there was a significantly lower CD68 ratio in the 60 cGy group compared to the 0 cGy group. Again, our mice are significantly aged, and inflammation would naturally be high, but 30 cGy of the mixed ion beam had a higher CD68 ratio compared to mice of the 60 cGy group which describes the inflammatory environment of an irradiated mouse with low tumor prevalence. Lipofuscin content followed this same data pattern and may be explained by its storage within giant multinucleated macrophages in aging ovaries, and CD68+ areas overlap with lipofuscin fluorescence [29, 81]. In the future it would be beneficial to study earlier timepoints and include the use of flow cytometry to gauge macrophage content involved in inflammatory responses in an ovary after heavy ion radiation treatment.

Overall, mice irradiated with 30 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam had the lowest prevalence of tumors of irradiated groups, highest prevalence of capsular hyperplasia of all experimental groups, and significantly elevated CD68-positive and lipofuscin-positive area when compared to mice irradiated with 60 cGy. By contrast, irradiation with 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam induced the highest prevalence of ovarian tumors and a lower prevalence of capsular hyperplasia compared to mice in the 30 cGy group. Additionally, mice irradiated with 60 cGy of the mixed heavy ion beam had significantly lower 4-HNE lipid peroxidation intensity and PSR-positive area compared to control.

The prospect of extended space exploration past the protective magnetic field of Earth will expose the growing cohort of female astronauts to GCRs on space missions. In this study, exposure to a mixed ion, 30 or 60 cGy beam consisting of Si, Ti, and Fe significantly depleted the ovarian follicle pool and induced ovarian tubular adenomas in a dose-dependent manner. Si irradiation alone at 32 cGy depleted ovarian follicles, but did not induce ovarian tumors. Ovarian tubular adenomas, of epithelial cell origin, are common in mice, but are not found in humans. Nonetheless, it is noteworthy that 90% of human ovarian tumors are classified as epithelial ovarian cancers [52]. Developing premature ovarian failure and ovarian cancer due to extended exposure to space radiation is a potentially significant threat to the health of the growing cohort of female astronauts. It is important that future animal studies consider the effect of the diverse quantity and composition of ions in GCRs, chronic low-dose rates, and microgravity to better model the effects of space travel on the ovary.
Single-cell transcriptomics of chicken ovarian cancer identifying immune subsets with prognostic implications

paper_metadata.title: Single-cell transcriptomics of chicken ovarian cancer identifying immune subsets with prognostic implications.

chunk: Ovarian cancer (OC) is a lethal gynecological malignancy with a low 5-year survival rate. The lack of preclinical models accurately capturing OC's early pathogenesis contributes to this poor prognosis. The domestic laying hen uniquely develops spontaneous OC, but its single-cell-level insights for pathogenesis have been lacking. Here, we present the first single-cell transcriptomic atlas of ovarian tissues from 110-week-old laying hens with or without OC. We annotated 12 core cellular lineages and characterized tumor-associated changes, including increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and reduced macrophages in OC samples. T cells sub-clustering revealed conserved cell subtype-specific pH homeostasis regulation profiles across species. Notably, gene signatures from the two dominant Cyto_CD8+ subsets exhibited opposing prognostic roles when validated against human OC datasets (GSE18520, GSE26712, GSE49997). This study confirms the laying hen as a valuable OC model by demonstrating cross-species conservation in cellular heterogeneity and oncogenic pathways, advancing it from a pathologically analogous system to a molecularly traceable tool.
Keywords: Laying hen, Ovarian cancer model; Single-cell transcriptomics

Epithelial ovarian cancer remains the deadliest gynecological malignancy, with approximately 70% of patients diagnosed at advanced-stage metastatic disease and a 5-year survival rate below 30% (Malvezzi et al., 2016; Webb and Jordan, 2024). Current preclinical models do not fully recapitulate this disease pathogenesis (Tsang, et al., 2022). Genetically engineered mouse models, such as MISRII-CRE-driven strains, and the chemically induced rat models, rarely develop spontaneous ovarian tumors (Lengyel, et al., 2014). Although 3D in vitro models effectively dissect cell-autonomous mechanisms, they lack the systemic tumor microenvironment essential for studying metastasis (Bradaric, et al., 2013).

The domestic laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) serves as a valuable model for ovarian cancer research (Bernardo, et al., 2015; Barua and Bahr, 2022; Johnson and Giles, 2013). This unique non-human species spontaneously develops epithelial ovarian cancer, with age-dependent incidence rates of 24% in 3.5-year-old hens and up to 60% in 4-year-old hens (Johnson and Giles, 2006, 2013). Critically, its reproductive biology aligns with Fathalla’s incessant ovulation hypothesis (Fathalla, 1971), mimicking the human reproductive risk profile through daily ovulation. Laying hen tumors recapitulate all major human histological subtypes, including serous, endometrioid, mucinous, and clear-cell carcinomas, and exhibit hallmark metastatic patterns such as intra-abdominal seeding and ascites accumulation (Barua, et al., 2009; Giles, et al., 2006;). This model enables investigation of early neoplastic events, such as preneoplastic dysplasia, which are inaccessible in humans (Barua, et al., 2009). Genetic strain differences in tumor susceptibility, such as the higher incidence observed in C strain compared to K strain among the laying hens, facilitate studies of heritable pathogenic mechanisms (Johnson and Giles, 2006).

The laying hen model offers significant translational value beyond elucidating carcinoma development mechanisms. Oral contraceptives demonstrate consistent protective effects across species. In humans, the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition confirmed their risk-lowering association with ovarian cancer (Tsilidis, et al., 2011) and a collaborative reanalysis of 45 studies reported a 40-50% risk reduction (Cancer, 2008). In laying hens, progestin alone or with estrogen decreases ovarian cancer prevalence by 91% and 81% respectively (Treviño, et al., 2012). Curcumin exhibits cross-species efficacy, modulating human-relevant oncogenic pathways, such as NF-κB and STAT3 inhibition, to reduce spontaneous ovarian cancer incidence by 57% in hens (Shi, et al., 2006; Sahin, et al., 2018). Flaxseed similarly aligns with human mechanisms, altering estrogen metabolism to promote 2-methoxyestradiol-induced apoptosis (Ansenberger, et al., 2010; Dikshit, et al., 2017; Fabová, et al., 2023; Keykhasalar, et al., 2021). Genistein also induces G2/M cell cycle arrest and apoptosis via DNA damage in humans (Gossner, et al., 2007; Lee, et al., 2012; Ouyang, et al., 2009), and reduces tumor incidence of 66.7% in hens by suppressing inflammatory cytokines and GSK-3 signaling (Erten, et al., 2021; Sahin, et al., 2019). Nanoparticle delivery further enhances translational potential, with doxorubicin-loaded nanoparticles eliminating patient-derived tumors in hen chorioallantois membranes while reducing toxicity (Chu, et al., 2022; Vu, et al., 2018). These consistent cross-species responses validate the laying hen as a critical preclinical tool for ovarian cancer therapeutics development.

Advances in omics have significantly advanced ovarian cancer research. Microarray analyses identified oviduct-related genes enriched in tumors of GSE21706 (Treviño, et al., 2010), and flaxseed-modulated genes linked to chemoprevention in GSE40376 (Hales, et al., 2014). Our prior comparative transcriptomics between hens and women revealed 81 conserved pathways and 174 core genes across species in GSE246604, highlighting GPR37 as a novel prognostic and immunotherapy biomarker in ovarian cancer (Zhu, et al., 2024). However, bulk RNA-seq data inherently fails to resolve intra-tumoral cellular heterogeneity, meaning these bulk analyses cannot capture cell-type-specific alterations critical for deciphering ovarian tumor heterogeneity (Hales, et al., 2014; Treviño, et al., 2010; Zhu, et al., 2024). Consequently, single-cell analysis of chicken ovarian tissues is urgently needed. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA-seq on ovarian tissues from 110-week-old hens with and without ovarian cancer, and establish cross-species cellular heterogeneity and oncogenic pathway comparisons. This approach thereby enhances the translational value of the laying hen as an ovarian cancer model.

Six 110-week-old Lohmann Layer strain hens were obtained from Runfeng Poultry Cooperative in Sichuan Province, China, including three healthy hens and three with ovarian cancer. All procedures complied with China's Ministry of Science and Technology Guidelines for Experimental Animals and were approved by the Sichuan University Animal Ethics Committee with permission ID SCU2203012.

Hens were euthanized via cervical dislocation with immediate ovarian tissue dissection on ice. Ovarian cancer staging followed morphological criteria from our previous study (Zhu, et al., 2024). Healthy ovaries featured intact follicular hierarchy including large preovulatory follicles and ordered small follicles. Ovarian cancer tissues were defined by solid nodular outgrowths, marked ovarian volume shrinkage, absence of large preovulatory follicles, and/or ascites. All ovarian cancer samples were classified as late-stage per these criteria. (Zhu, et al., 2024). For single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), three biological replicates each of healthy ovarian tissues and ovarian cancer tissues, were selected and immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. These samples were sent to SHBIO Biotechnology Co. Ltd. for processing using the DNBelab C series platform from BGI Genomics.

Tissue dissociation and single-cell suspension preparation were conducted by BGI Genomics following their standardized protocol for fresh solid tissues using the DNBelab C series platform (Han, et al., 2022; Wang, et al., 2021a; Zhu, et al., 2023). Frozen tissues were thawed and minced into 1–2 mm³ fragments, digested with collagenase IV and hyaluronidase at 37°C for 25 minutes, and filtered through 70 μm and 40 μm strainers to remove debris. Cells were resuspended in 1× phosphate-buffered saline with 0.04% BSA, and viability and concentration (600–1000 cells/μL) verified using a Countess II Automated Cell Counter (Invitrogen). scRNA-seq libraries were constructed using the BGI Single Cell Gene Expression Library Prep Kit (Senabouth, et al., 2020; Wang, et al., 2021b). Qualified single-cell suspensions were loaded onto a BGI Single Cell Chip to generate gel beads-in-emulsion for barcoded cDNA synthesis. Libraries were quantified using a Qubit 4.0 Fluorometer, then sequenced on an BGI500 platform.

Raw data preprocessing including quality control, adapter trimming and alignment, were performed by BGI Genomics. Low-quality reads were filtered with FastQC (Wingett and Andrews, 2018). Clean reads were aligned to the Gallus gallus reference genome using Hisat2 (Kim, et al., 2019). Cell-gene count matrices were generated with Htseq (Anders, et al., 2015). Sequencing data supporting this study have been deposited into CNSA (https://db.cngb.org/) with accession number CNP0008144.

Count matrices were imported into Seurat 4.4 for downstream analysis (Stuart, et al., 2019). Doublet detection was performed using the scDblFinder package to identify potential cell doublets (Germain, et al., 2022), which were excluded before quality control. Cells were filtered to remove low-quality populations, which defined those with fewer than 200 detected genes, more than 6000 detected genes, or more than 10% mitochondrial RNA were excluded (Stuart, et al., 2019). Qualified cells underwent normalized using LogNormalize, and 2000 highly variable genes were selected via variance stabilizing transformation (VST) for dimensionality reduction (Stuart, et al., 2019).

Principal Component Analysis was performed using the selected highly variable genes, and the top 15 principal components (determined via elbow plot analysis) were used for Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualization (Stuart, et al., 2019). Cells were clustered using the Louvain algorithm at resolution 0.2 via Seurat’s FindClusters function (Stuart, et al., 2019).

Differential gene expression between healthy and ovarian cancer cell populations was identified using Seurat’s FindMarkers function (Stuart, et al., 2019). Genes were considered differentially expressed if they met the criteria of adjusted p < 0.05 and absolute log₂ fold change ( log₂FC ) > 0.25. Volcano plots illustrating DGE results were generated using the ggpubr package (Blighe, et al., 2019; Kassambara, 2018).

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) for KEGG pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) was performed using the clusterProfiler package [7]. Visualization of enrichment results was done with ggpubr (Kassambara, 2018).

T cells were subclustered from the integrated dataset using Seurat’s Subset function, and re-clustered with the Louvain algorithm at resolution 0.8 to generate 16 distinct subclusters. Co-expression analysis of key marker genes was performed using Seurat’s FeaturePlot function, with visualization at a color threshold of 0.2.

Single-sample GSEA (ssGSEA) was performed using the GSVA (Hänzelmann, et al., 2013) to calculate enrichment scores of chicken Cyto_CD8⁺_2 and Cyto_CD8⁺_3 subcluster signatures in human ovarian cancer datasets (GSE18520, GSE27651, GSE49997). Patients were stratified into high- and low-score groups using the median score as the cutoff. Kaplan-Meier survival curves and log-rank tests were conducted with the survival and survminer packages to assess associations between signature scores and overall survival (Therneau and Lumley, 2015).

All statistical analyses were performed using R 4.2.2 with significance set at p < 0.05. Cell type/subcluster proportion differences between healthy and cancerous tissues were tested via Pearson’s χ² test. DGE was determined using the MAST test (adjusted p < 0.05, log₂FC > 0.25) in Seurat (Stuart, et al., 2019). GSEA used 1000 permutations with clusterProfiler, with enriched terms defined by NES > 1.2 or < −1.2, p < 0.05. ssGSEA score comparisons between human tumor/normal tissues or high/low patient groups were done via Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and survival associations were evaluated with log-rank tests using the survival package (Hänzelmann, et al., 2013; Therneau and Lumley, 2015; Wu, et al., 2021). Multiple testing correction was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.

To delineate cellular heterogeneity between healthy chicken ovaries and ovarian cancer samples, we first acquired fresh tissue samples, where the healthy ovaries exhibited well-organized follicular structures, whereas the ovarian cancer samples displayed disorganized tumor masses (Fig. 1A). After cell filtering, scRNA-seq yielded 23,412 cells from healthy ovaries designated as 110w_normal_ovary and 13,167 cells from ovarian cancer tissues designated as 110w_ovarian_cancer (Fig. 1B). UMAP dimensionality reduction revealed distinct clustering patterns between the two groups (Fig. 1B). Integrating all cells (n = 30,822), we annotated major cell lineages using canonical marker genes (Fig. 1C and 1D), including CD4⁺ T cells (CD3D, CD3E, CD4), CD8⁺ T cells (CD3D, CD3E, CD8A), B cells (CD77B, PAX5, CD74), plasma cells (JCHAIN, XBP1), macrophages (C1QB, C1QC), epithelial cells (KRT7, KRT18), granulosa cells (AMH, GATA4, RLN3, WNT4), theca cells (CYP11A1, CYP17A1, LHCGR, STAR), fibroblasts (ACTA2, TAGLN, DCN), and endothelial cells (CDH5, PECAM1, VMF). Dot plots validated these annotations, with lineage-specific markers showing cell type-specific expression (Fig. 1D).

Immune cells are a key component of the tumor microenvironment, and their dynamic remodeling directly regulates tumor progression and therapeutic responsiveness. UMAP visualization highlighted their distribution in healthy ovaries versus ovarian cancer samples (Fig. 2A). Quantitative analysis revealed significant immune subpopulation shifts, with ovarian cancer showing reduced macrophages but increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (p = 4.17e-111; Fig. 2B). Differential gene expression analyses uncovered distinct transcriptional profiles across immune subsets. CD8+ T cells exhibited 101 upregulated genes in ovarian cancer versus 61 in normal ovaries (Fig. 2C). CD4⁺ T cells showed 57 upregulated genes in cancer versus 32 in healthy ovaries (Fig. 2D). Macrophages displayed 199 upregulated genes in cancer versus 83 in healthy ovaries (Fig. 2E). B cells had 18 upregulated genes in cancer versus 5 in healthy ovaries (Fig. 2F). Plasma cells exhibited 197 upregulated genes in cancer versus 54 in healthy ovaries (Fig. 2G). Total immune cells showed 646 upregulated genes in cancer versus 637 in healthy ovaries (Fig. 2H).

Beyond immune cells, epithelial cells, stromal cells, and granulosa cells also contribute to tumor progression within the tumor microenvironment. As shown in Fig. 3A and 3B, the epithelial cells exhibited extensive differential gene expression (DGE) in ovarian cancer, with 233 genes upregulated in ovarian cancer whereas 366 genes upregulated in normal ovaries. For stromal & granulosa cells (including granulosa, theca, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells; Fig. 3C), the DGE analysis revealed that endothelial cells had 45 genes upregulated in ovarian cancer while 167 genes upregulated in normal ovaries (Fig. 3D). The fibroblasts showed 93 genes upregulated in ovarian cancer and 129 genes upregulated in normal ovaries (Fig. 3E). As sown in Fig. 3F and 3G, the Granulosa_1 cells exhibited 3002 genes upregulated in ovarian cancer and 987 genes upregulated in normal ovaries. In contrast, the Granulosa_2 cells had 178 genes upregulated in ovarian cancer and 58 genes upregulated in normal ovaries. Theca_2 cells displayed 25 genes upregulated in ovarian cancer and 20 genes upregulated in normal ovaries (Fig. 3H).

To delineate cell-type-specific functional remodeling in ovarian carcinogenesis, we conducted the pathway enrichment analyses. The top-ranked pathways across different cell lineages were prioritized with the distinct top two GO pathways exhibited. As shown in Fig. 4A, the B cells showed the enrichment in cytoskeletal motor activity and signaling receptor regulator activity. The CD4+_T cells were enriched in regulation of GTPase activity and axon guidance. The CD8+_T cells displayed enrichment in chromosome, centromeric region and cell fate commitment. The Endothelial cells were enriched in cytosolic ribosome and nuclear chromosome. The Epithelial cells showed the enrichment in external encapsulating structure and steroid metabolic process. The fibroblasts were enriched in cell-cell adhesion mediator activity and modulation of chemical synaptic. The Granulosa_1 cells exhibited enrichment in DNA-binding transcription factor activity, RNA polymerase II-specific and transforming growth factor beta receptor superfamily signaling pathway. The Granulosa_2 cells were enriched in postsynaptic density and regulation of membrane potential. The Granulosa_3 cells showed enrichment in respiratory electron transport chain and structural constituent of ribosome. The Macrophages were enriched in cytokine activity and RNA helicase activity. The Plasma cells exhibited enrichment in organelle fusion and cell cycle process. Theca_1 cells were enriched in cytosolic small ribosomal subunit and sterol biosynthetic process. Theca_2 cells showed the enrichment in oxidative phosphorylation and iron ion binding.

Given the critical role of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment, we further focused on CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and macrophages for further GSEA core enrichment analyses, where the most significant genes were listed. As shown in Fig. 4B, the CD4+_T cells showed the pathways enriched in cancer, including cell differentiation (PLXNA2, RBPMS2, SIPA1, LAMA5, VDR, BEND6), multicellular organism development, anatomical structure morphogenesis, neurogenesis, regulation of GTPase activity. In healthy ovaries, CD4+_T cells favored the pathways related to organelle lumen, nuclear lumen, ribosome biogenesis, rRNA processing and steroid biosynthetic process (LBR, FDFT1, LSS, INIG1, SQLE, HSD17B7). In CD8+_T cells, as shown in Fig. 4C, the cancer-enriched pathways included cellular developmental process, cell differentiation (PCK2, MYL2, LAMA1, HEY2, RBPMS2, WNT4), response to nutrient levels, ECM-receptor interaction, cell fate commitment, were revealed to be enriched in the ovarian cancer samples. In contrast, the CD8+_T cells from the healthy ovaries showed the enrichment in immune system process, myeloid leukocyte migration, sterol metabolic process (HSD17B7, LBR, CYP11A1, MSMO1, INSIG1, DHCR7) and cell cycle G2/M phase transition, steroid biosynthesis (HSD17B7, LBR, DHCR24, CYP51A1, NSDHL, MSMO1), chromosome segregation. In Macrophages, as shown in Fig. 4D, the cancer-enriched pathways including the G protein-coupled receptor signaling pathway (ADGRA2, ACKR4, CX3CL1, IL8L1, ENDRA, SPNS2), WNT signaling pathway (WNT4, WNT6, ADGRA2, AXIN2, CTNNBIP1, TLE3), growth factor binding, cytokine receptor activity, leukocyte chemotaxis, were enriched in chicken ovarian cancer samples. And the healthy ovarian macrophages were enriched in positive regulation of biosynthetic process, methyltransferase activity, membrane-enclosed lumen, monoatomic ion homeostasis, monoatomic ion homeostasis and RNA helicase activity.

T cells serve as central effector cells mediating anti-tumor immune responses, and exhibit significant functional heterogeneity. To resolve this heterogeneity in ovarian carcinogenesis, we performed T cell subclustering, identifying 16 distinct subclusters visualized by UMAP (Fig. 5A). These subclusters were annotated by cell type and functional identity, including five cytotoxic CD8+ (Cyto_CD8+) subsets, proliferating CD8+, Helper CD4+, Memory CD4+, Naive CD4+, and regulatory T (Treg) lineages (Fig. 5B). Comparative analysis of T cell subtype proportions revealed statistically significant shifts between healthy ovaries and ovarian cancer tissues (overall Chi-square p = 2.05e-67). The Cyto_CD8+_2 and Cyto_CD8+_3 showed the most pronounced differences (P = 2.45e-39 and P = 1.03e-33, respectively) (Fig. 5C). Volcano plot analysis of Cyto_CD8+_2 versus Cyto_CD8+_3 identified 49 genes upregulated in Cyto_CD8+_2 cells and 17 genes upregulated in Cyto_CD8+_3 cells (Fig. 5D). For Cyto_CD8+_2 cells, the gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA, Fig. 5E) in ovarian cancer showed enriched pathways including PPAR signaling pathway (ACAA1A, APOA1, PDPK1, ACSL5, DBI, ME3), G protein-coupled receptor activity, regulation of DNA repair, regulation of intracellular pH (ATP6V0D1, SLC4A2, SLC4A1, ATP6V0A2), and immune response. Healthy ovary-derived Cyto_CD8⁺_2 cells featured cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway, smoothened signaling pathway, endosome organization, sulfur amino acid metabolic process, and DNA-templated transcription initiation. For the Cyto_CD8+_3 cells, as shown in Fig. 5F, ovarian cancer enrichment included G protein-coupled receptor activity, ECM-receptor interaction, Neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, animal organ development and microtubule bundle formation to be enriched. While healthy ovary enrichment involved ubiquitin-protein transferase activity, GTPase binding, regulation of pH (SLC9A7, SLC4A2, DMXL1, ATP6V0D1, SLC9A6, SLC4A8), ubiquitin biosynthetic process, positive regulation of proteolysis. UMAP-based gene co-expression mapping confirmed CST7 and FKBP5 as markers co-localizing specifically to Cyto_CD8+_2 (Fig. 5G), while EOMES and IL2RB co-localized to Cyto_CD8+_3 (Fig. 5H), validating these pairs as definitive identifiers for the two dominant cytotoxic CD8+ T cell subsets in ovarian carcinogenesis.

To translate chicken ovarian cancer findings to humans, we applied single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) to assess the signature enrichment of chicken Cyto_CD8+_2 and Cyto_CD8+_3 in human datasets (GSE18520, GSE26712, GSE49997). In GSE18520, Cyto_CD8⁺_2 signature scores were significantly higher in human ovarian tumors than in normal tissues (p = 0.005), while Cyto_CD8⁺_3 scores were elevated in normal tissues (p = 1.1e-05) (Fig. 6A). Similar patterns were observed in GSE26712, where the Cyto_CD8+_2 scores showed tumor enrichment (p = 0.025) and Cyto_CD8+_3 scores showed normal enrichment (p = 3.8e-07) (Fig. 6B). Subsequent survival analysis using GSE49997 demonstrated that low Cyto_CD8⁺_2 scores correlated with poorer overall prognosis (Fig. 6C; log-rank p = 0.045), with a median survival time of 34.0 months versus not reached for low versus high groups (Fig. 6C). Conversely, high Cyto_CD8⁺_3 scores (Fig. 6D) were associated with poorer prognosis (log-rank p = 0.042), showing a median survival time of 44.0 months versus not reached for high versus low groups. Significant differences confirmed conserved, opposing prognostic roles for these cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cell subclusters in ovarian cancer.

Molecular characterization of ovarian cancer mechanisms enables precision breeding for ovarian cancer-resistant chicken lines, directly reducing economic losses in poultry production. This study presents the first single-cell transcriptomic atlas of ovarian tissues from 110-week-old laying hens in both ovarian cancer and heathy groups (Johnson and Giles, 2013; Niebora, et al., 2024). We annotated 12 core cellular lineages encompassing immune, epithelial and stromal cells were annotated (Fig. 1C-D). Tumor-associated shifts included increased CD4+/CD8+ T cells and reduced macrophages, along with cell-type-specific transcriptional reprogramming were revealed. Our study identified 16 T cell subsets, revealing conserved pH homeostasis regulation in Cyto_CD8+ populations, and validated the opposing prognostic roles of Cyto_CD8+_2 and Cyto_CD8+_3 signatures in human ovarian cancer. This atlas provides a foundational framework for dissecting cell origins and heterogeneity in spontaneous ovarian tumors, advancing the laying hen from a pathologically analogous model to a molecularly traceable tool (Barua and Bahr, 2022; Niebora, et al., 2024).

Chicken ovarian cancer shows immune dynamics closely aligned with human ovarian cancer, validating the model’s biological relevance. Chicken ovarian cancer exhibits increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proportions and decreased macrophages (Fig. 2B), mirroring the immune-infiltrated subtype observed in human ovarian cancer (Hornburg, et al., 2021; Yang, et al., 2024). Epithelial cells in chickens enrich extracellular matrix-related pathways (Fig. 4A), consistent with epithelial-mesenchymal transition in human ovarian cancer (Winterhoff, et al., 2017). Human single-cell studies identify similar epithelial-stromal heterogeneity (Winterhoff, et al., 2017), linking stromal cell states to tumor grade (Shih, et al., 2018). Recurrent immune subsets were characterized in both high-grade serous ovarian cancer (Gonzalez, et al., 2018). In chickens, granulosa cell subpopulations show extensive transcriptional reprogramming in tumors, with Granulosa_1 cells exhibiting 3,002 upregulated genes in ovarian cancer versus 987 in normal ovaries (Fig. 3F), echoing granulosa-like stromal remodeling in human ovarian cancer (Shih, et al., 2018). These parallels support the chicken model for ovarian cancer pathogenesis studies.

Present study validates the chicken model through conserved molecular pathways. Classic ovarian cancer biomarkers show cross-species consistency with CA125, a key human diagnostic marker, in spontaneous chicken ovarian adenocarcinomas and cultured chicken ovarian cancer cells (Jackson, et al., 2007). p53 mutations occur in 48% of chicken tumors, matching the high mutation rate in human cases (Hakim, et al., 2009). E-cadherin shows higher mRNA and protein expression in chicken cancerous ovaries versus normal tissues (Ansenberger, et al., 2009), consistent with its upregulation in human primary ovarian tumors (Ansenberger, et al., 2009). Aquaporin 5, which functions in water transport and cellular proliferation, shows abnormal expression in both chicken ovarian tumors and human ovarian cancer (Tiwari, et al., 2014; Yang, et al., 2006). We identified the conserved pH homeostasis regulation, a critical process for tumor cell survival and drug resistance (Sanhueza, et al., 2016; Webb, et al., 2011). Chicken Cyto_CD8+_2 cells in ovarian cancer enrich pH regulation pathways via genes including ATP6V0D1, SLC4A2, SLC4A1, and ATP6V0A2 (Fig. 5E), while Cyto_CD8⁺_3 cells in healthy ovaries utilize pH regulation genes such as SLC9A7, SLC4A2, DMXL1, ATP6V0D1, SLC9A6, and SLC4A8 (Fig. 5F). This cancer-specific pH dysregulation aligns with human ovarian cancer mechanisms. The genes of pH regulation pathway were also mapped to the pathways with established roles in human ovarian cancer, where the SLC4A family members contributing to epithelial-stromal crosstalk in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (Gonzalez, et al., 2018; Qin, et al., 2017), and V-ATPase subunits like ATP6V0A2 linking to serous ovarian cancer pathogenesis (Salvi, et al., 2022). Classic oncogenic pathways converge across species. WNT signaling, activated in chicken macrophages (Fig. 4D), links to human high-grade serous ovarian cancer initiation (Arend, et al., 2013; Teeuwssen and Fodde, 2019). T cell receptor signaling in chicken CD8+ T cells (Fig. 4C) mirrors its role as a hallmark of high T cell infiltration in human (Olalekan, et al., 2021). NF-kB and STAT3 pathways, targeted by flaxseed to reduce chicken tumor incidence (Ansenberger, et al., 2010; Hales, et al., 2014), are well-characterized oncogenic pathways in human ovarian cancer (Stepień, et al., 2025). miR-200 family governs ovarian cancer spreading and serves as a blood biomarker in humans (Choi and Ng, 2017), with conserved functions and biomarker potential in chickens (Choi, et al., 2020a, 2020b). Cyclooxygenase expression dysregulation in chicken ovarian cancer (Hales, et al., 2008; Urick and Johnson, 2006), is consistent with its role in human disease (Daikoku, et al., 2005; Gupta et al., 2003).

Present study also confirms the translational relevance of chicken-derived cell subcluster signatures through cross-species ssGSEA. The chicken Cyto_CD8+_2 signature is enriched in human tumors, while the Cyto_CD8+_3 signature is enriched in normal human tissues (Fig. 5A, 5B). This pattern is consistent with the findings in human (Olbrecht, et al., 2021; Xu, et al., 2022). Survival analysis revealed their opposing prognostic roles, where the low Cyto_CD8+_2 scores or high Cyto_CD8+_3 scores correlate with poorer overall survival (Fig. 6C, 6D), aligning with T cell subpopulations dictating prognosis in human metastatic ovarian cancer (Deng, et al., 2022; Olalekan, et al., 2021).
